Similarly, Daniel Penny, a veteran and student, couldn't trust that Jordan Neely wouldn't harm him or anyone else on that train or that help was ever coming.

comments.name: Kevin Moran
comments.body: This article points to a serious problem, but it leaves out an important part of the conversation, and that is the role of parents. We spend a lot of time discussing what schools, teachers, administrators, and government officials should do differently. Those questions are valid, but schools cannot solve everything on their own. Parents need to be actively involved in their children’s education. They should know whether their children are attending school, completing assignments, reading regularly, learning basic math, behaving appropriately, and making progress. That means communicating with teachers, attending conferences, setting expectations at home, limiting distractions, and showing through their actions that education matters. Too often, we act as though responsibility for a child’s success transfers entirely to the school once the child enters the classroom. It does not. Public schools are responsible for educating children, but they cannot also be expected to raise them. Accountability has to go both ways. We should expect excellent teachers, strong curricula, safe classrooms, capable administrators, and measurable results from our schools. We should also expect parents to take an active role in their children’s education and development. If America wants to reverse these academic trends, improving schools is only part of the answer. We also need to rebuild a culture in which parents, students, and schools each accept their share of responsibility.

Against this backdrop, one could argue that increasingly apocalyptic narratives about AI also serve to manage public and investor expectations. The mistake, however, is anthropomorphizing AI and shifting responsibility onto inanimate software. The real concern should be the very human decisions made by CEOs and policymakers, including whether adequate protections are established for workers affected by AI-driven automation.

China may likewise be operating in a gray area, issuing warnings while confronting its own automation challenges and demographic pressures. And when major AI companies in Silicon Valley or Wall Street promise to “slow down,” I would interpret such claims cautiously: research and development may continue accelerating with less public exposure. After the midterm elections, market conditions could stabilize and strategies for going public could change again.

There is no realistic way to reverse AI progress. Believing that technological development can simply be turned back is a fool’s dream.

The Five Ws and one H of clear and effective journalism:

Who – the people, groups, or organizations involved or affected

What – the event, action, or situation

When – the time it happened or will happen

Where – the location(s) involved

Why – the reasons, causes, or motivations behind it

The One H is:

How – the methods, processes, or means by which it happened 

Together, these six questions form a checklist to ensure a story is complete, clear, and self-contained, often in the lead paragraph.

Capture all essential facts in a concise lead

Maintain clarity and completeness in reporting

Help readers understand the full context without extra searching 

It’s also a tool for fact-checking and critical thinking, ensuring no key detail is overlooked.

Origins
The concept has ancient roots in Greek rhetoric (Hermagoras of Temnos, 1st century BC).

. In modern journalism, it was formalized in the early 20th century and popularized in the U.S. by 1917. 

This ensures the reader gets the full story in the first sentences.

I defrost in the refrigerator in a plastic container. I then remove scales under running water using only fingers going in the opposite direction of the scales. I then cut the head, tail and belly section off to remove the entrails. At this point, do not wash them. Any water in an open fish will saturate the flesh and prevent it from crisping under heat. Clean with paper towel instead. If you want to remove the bone, slide your finger (beginning at the tail section) along the spine and it will separate without breaking the fish. comments.name: Papaya
comments.body:
Reading this and listening to the interview with Coxon on The Daily gives me bit of a reminder of the pre quakes ahead of the credit crisis.

There were warning signs about the financial weapons of mass destruction---CDOs and other structured products constructed with low-quality mortgages---yet the producers kept on selling them and the investors kept buying them. This is exactly what Kitroeff asks Coxon---"Why keep make something when you know it could lead to the demise of all humans?"

While working for an asset manager during the beginning of the credit crisis, a client asked our chief credit officer why we would invest client money if we knew these products were garbage. He answered too honestly, "because all our clients were demanding it and to remain competitive we had to provide them. We had no choice." 

This is absolutely the gamble the world is facing now: for an advanced economy to remain competitive it has to win the AI race. I am not hopeful that governments will be prepared this time to understand a technology before it destroys the lives of everyday people---economically or physically. They've been flatfooted before in the face of known risks and if Republicans and Democrats can't even collaborate on simple policies (heck, even among themselves!), how can we trust them to collaborate on more complex ones?

Bob Mackie was an absolutely unique and super-talented costume and fashion designer, and a true American original.  He also seemed like a rather nice person which is far from a given if you know anything about the fashion industry and those that work in it.  His style was distinctive and timeless - his costumes for Cher, Carol Burnett and others speak for themselves in their sexy yet tasteful and elegant designs.  Truly unique.

HBO did a recent biography of Mackie.  I was disappointed to learn of his estranged relationship with his only son who died in 1993.  His granddaughter appears in the documentary and, until recently, had no contact with her grandfather, apparently at his request.  The insinuation is that perhaps she was after money, which was not the case. She wanted to know her grandfather and I felt bad watching the scene play out, it made me uncomfortable.  This is personal stuff and I wish it weren't in the film because, since I'm only human, I couldn't help but view him less enthusiastically after learning this stuff.  I always find it very distasteful to learn that parents abandon their children or grandchildren and view them as an inconvenience rather than a blessing.

But getting back to his accomplishments, they were truly remarkable.  His Academy Award nomination for Funny Lady was well earned.  Pity he was up against Barry Lyndon that year because Streisand never looked more beautiful than she did in that film, all thanks to his gorgeous designs.

comments.name: Prof. John G. Cramer
comments.body: IMHO, the unlikely history of the development of life on Earth is quite discouraging for the prospects of finding anything beyond bacteria elsewhere in our galaxy.  Our planet was the target of a low-probability Late Heavy Bombardment that supplied lots of water for our oceans from comets outside the Ice Line and that provided the four critical biomolecules needed for forming RNA.  Then the RNA had to develop self-replication.  Then the self-replicating RNA had to learn to assemble amino acids to make proteins.  Then the proteins had to somehow make bacteria.  Then things came to a halt for a couple of billion years, until one suffocating hydrogen-breathing protocell captured an oxygen-breathing bacterium that became the mitochondria of all eukaryotes, including us.  That was an extremely unlikely event.  Without some chain of low-probability events like this, no exoplanet, whether in its parent star's habitable zone or not, will have any higher multicellular life forms.  I would love to live in a galaxy populated with interesting intelligent aliens, but I think our planet Earth must be unique in our galaxy in having intelligent life.  We had better take care of it!

I was attending a state university in the late 1960s and had a student deferment like all men attending college.  This deferment remained valid as long as I “was making satisfactory progress toward a degree.”  

Then I dropped low in credits one quarter and was immediately summoned for a military physical to which I reported, and given one more quarter to make up the deficiency.  I did so and saved my deferment.  Had I failed to do so I would have been immediately eligible for the draft.

Had I not reported for the physical the machinery of the State would have put me on a wanted list and my freedom would soon have ended.  I see here where the photographer Vlad has dodged his physical and is now understandingly nervous about his prospects going forward.  But don’t think that this is some kind of totalitarian terror. comments.body: I feel like there isn’t necessarily a reason to stop watching or playing football, aside from the obvious injuries, but I feel like football has been idolized in the United States to the point that it’s beginning to become detrimental to Americans. In general, sports are an amazing space to have a conversation point, something entertaining that is always online, and a place where you are accepted by fellow supporters. But unlike most sports, football takes this to a whole new level. Football takes what is supposed to be a fun, entertaining game into an apocalypse of competition. The appeal to football, passed through generations, cities, and schools, is rooted in one thing: ethnocentrism. Americans, years and years ago, wanted their own sport, for Americans only. Therefore, Americans found excessive pride in their city’s team, along with football as a whole, eventually transitioning to excessive sports gambling, fights based on which teams you support, and spending each day falling victim to checking your Fantasy points, in fear of whatever humiliating punishment is in store. Not to mention that these sports teams’ players who don’t even get on the field often get paid more than first responders, educators, and nonprofit workers. comments.body: My main goal for this year is to be more in the present in my everyday life. I agree with Dunn about the fact that September has a new start effect. September is the gateway to fall and winter and that is the perfect time to start my new goals as the days get colder and shorter and as I spend more time inside. For me it is hard to be present sometimes in this world full of distractions like social media. Most importantly, I want to take a few steps back and look at where I am currently because in the past I’ve spent more time waiting for what's next just to miss out on the present. I email teachers, prepare my club for activities, and, if needed, buy new supplies for myself. I believe September is more representative of new beginnings than January.

comments.body: I agree with her point saying that September is a new January, and a lot of her points make sense. It's much easier to start a routine if you can do it at your own pace without being crowded. comments.name: Gabi
comments.body: When it comes to years to me I think of it beginning in September, ending in May, and the summer is just its own thing. As the new school year comes around each September it feels as though there is so much possibility. You get to catch up with classmates, who you maybe have not seen since the beginning of June, at the end of last school year. January falls right in the middle of the school year, so there is nothing new except maybe some new snow every couple weeks. As Laura Vanderkam says, you just “have more energy after a restful summer.” In my opinion it is much easier to accomplish new goals in September when I have more energy, than it is in January when it seems that the school year is never going to end.

comments.name: Rylie Haynie
comments.body:
When looking at the start of the school year, the amount of things you have ahead of you can be overwhelming. You get huge lists of tasks and rapidly approaching deadlines, but it’s designed to give you the most out of your time. 
Dunn quotes Jim Kwik “Write down a few things you’d like to learn, then see which ones you can realistically put into action.” This idea perfectly encapsulates the steps we take to get through the year. Realistically, five to seven classes a day, plus college applications, plus personal projects and portfolios can pile up staggeringly fast, but by breaking it down into one small task at a time we can grant ourselves the space to get it all done. For many of us, college early access deadlines end in December so the start of school in August can put a wrench in the plan, but the best tool at one’s disposal is good time management skills.

comments.body:
The BOJ may want to try raising interest rates on savings accounts after having them decoupled from its policy rates and market yield rates. The BOJ could then allow banks to compete for deposits and subsequently adjust the reserve requirement ratio. If executed correctly, this strategy could effectively help remove money from circulation and control the re-entry of capital loosely into the market, resulting in deflationary effects without requiring a policy rate hike. In my view, a little bit of creative thinking and an open-minded approach may help us see other interesting strategies to solve economic problems besides relying solely on traditional, conventional methods like adjusting short-term policy rates.

I believe one major factor keeping pressure on the JPY is Japan’s heavy reliance on foreign energy imports denominated in USD, especially amid the current uncertainty surrounding the oil market. In contrast, as a net oil-exporting and energy self-sufficient nation, the U.S. is in a much more stable position than much of the rest of the world, and this structural advantage will likely persist despite the ongoing uncertainty, strengthening the USD against the currencies of energy-dependent nations. Ipso facto, Japan should expedite its joint stockpile and crude reserve expansion deals with Arab nations. I believe obtaining more strategic oil reserves and securing emergency access to a stable supply could help strengthen Japan’s currency.

The country gets considerable support from Russia and still has vestiges of sclerotic bureaucracy in some of its institutions.    Some of the main streets are beautiful, wide boulevards flanked by towering trees.    A good amount of parks, although some were sorely in need of renovation.   
Kyrgyzstan will likely remain tied to China and Russia, both of which border it.    It makes far more sense to ally yourself with your neighbors than a distant (and currently unreliable) power from the other side of the world.

A Sonnet, Slightly Out of Tune

A fourteen-lined design of metred verse,
Where iambs march in steady, patterned stride,
To frame a thought, a blessing, or a curse,
With secrets that the final lines decide.

It opens with a formal, strict constraint,
Where rhyming pairs construct a clever cage,
To sing a lover’s heavy, sweet complaint,
Or capture fleeting beauty on the page.

But look! The rigid rules must now give way,
A dis-so-nant dis-cord may split the chord,
To show how human passions truly play,
Before the final harmony's restored.

For flawless songs are cold and empty things;
It is the cracked and wounded heart that sings.

I was across the way from the  Pentagon on 911.  I didn't lose anyone but I felt terrible loss.  Actually I felt it two nights before it happened. I was overwhelmed with feelings of imminent tragedy.  I was so distraught I pulled off I 270 and called home to tell my wife "Something is terribly wrong".
I never overcome that feeling. Since the beginning of the 2nd Trump administration I've had that same feeling of dread and loss time and again.  
There IS something wrong in the universe. Trump is going to cause us terrible loss. I feel it deep, deep inside.  When I saw my mother for the first time after 911 she said to me "Look what they've done to my New York".  Mom was born in Brooklyn in 1923 and in December 1941 recalled the attack on Pearl Harbor.  She felt at 911 the same way she felt on December 7th 1941.  She was young then in her first year of college and as soon as she was old enough she enlisted in the Navy WAVES.  Her father had to sign permission for her.  The emotions and the feelings of loss of December 1941 never left her.  Joining the Navy helped her deal with 1941.  
In 2001 I was 54. I was too old to rejoin the Army and witnessing the Pentagon being struck sickened me. Twenty years later I still feel that way.  I don't have any choices to make. Except for one.
I don't want to see the politicians in power who were never able to deal with such an enormous tragedy that we can't erase.
I will chose to vote for people to end the endless carnage that followed 911.

I note in particular that the Great Depression was the main feature of the interwar period.  We have not had another Great Depression, yet.  As an anecdotal side note, it seems to be easier and cheaper to buy politicians than in the past.

The second reason is that he appears to succumb to group think (advertising narratives) about the rationality of conservatism.  Conservatives are entirely about their feels (need to feel "up").  The essential elements of conservatism (feel "up" and escape responsibility) inevitably devolve into nihilism.  Because destruction is easier than construction.  Given the combined mechanical advantage of the destructiveness of conservatism and the effects of climate change, it is important to properly weight how easy it will be to make the earth unlivable for homo sapiens and the innumerable creatures that homo sapiens depends on to live as we currently do.

I like Mr. Laska's  advice to use pothos as a learning gateway. So often new plant owners don't spend time observing and actually tending their plants, so an infestation or a problem gets out of control before they realize it. Pothos tells you what's happening pretty fast, and responds to remedies quickly.

One thing newbies seem to hesitate about is sticking their fingers in the soil. They always want to know, do I water once a week? Every three days? But conditions in your room will change (and as your plant grows, the root/soil ratio and leaf volume will, too) and the only way to know what your plant needs is to get an actual sense of the soil conditions. comments.body:
May I say right off the bat?  

You are one heck of a writer, Mr. Garner.  

So thank you.  

But here you're casting a rather dour, unappreciative eye upon the landscape--

--or should I say, the soundscape?

--of yesteryear.  The weird fads.  The fashions.  The personalities.  And how to say this?  

The sheer noise!  

But isn't that true of human beings.  We make so much noise.  We're all talking at once.  And at the top of our lungs.  Or we're singing.  Or trying to sing--

--'cause we were assured by someone we had talent.  

Yeah, right! 

And then--puff, the magic dragon!  It all fades away.  Or rather, it's displaced by the fads and whims of a later day and age.  The personalities get old and die.  Or dwindle into a long, regretful retirement.    

Or they write memoirs.  Or collect their earlier writings and  take an editor's pencil to this or that.  A blundering epithet.  An ill-advised opinion.  An ineptly chosen noun.  

But the noise goes on.  And on.  

You know something?  I was struck by Mr. Stahl's rather poignant remark, quoted at the close of your piece.  

--"Maybe that's as close to happiness as you get--

"--not making other people unhappy."  

I turned seventy seven last month, Mr. Garner.  

And, if by a bit of beneficent magic, I could recall or undo the unhappiness I've caused other people--

--I'd be the happiest man on the planet.  

Thanks again.

comments.body: Surrogates (also called “gestational carriers” or GCs) in the real world must wait a year between pregnancies; even if you have perfect pregnancies, the limit is 6, including your own kids. You need to be done having your own family first; be financially stable (not counting on your surrogacy pay to feed your family, eg) and undergo psych and medical screening. Many try to be surrogates; few are accepted. And because old stories (“Baby M”) are stuck in some heads, modern surrogacy almost never entails the surrogate having a genetic link to the child; in fact, that’s illegal now in most states.
